title: The Mind of Christ, Who Emptied Himself
summary: Paul appeals to the Philippians to be united in love and humility, each looking to the interests of others. He grounds the appeal in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, did not grasp at equality with God but emptied himself, took the form of a servant, and humbled himself to death on a cross, and whom God therefore exalted and gave the name above every name, so that every knee will bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord. Paul then urges them to work out their salvation as God works in them, to shine as lights in a crooked generation, and commends Timothy and Epaphroditus, two men who live out the same self-giving pattern.
story: Chapter 1 ended with a call to stand firm in one spirit against outside opposition. Chapter 2 turns inward to the church's own unity, which was apparently strained (4:2-3 names two leaders at odds). Paul's answer is not a technique for resolving conflict but a portrait of Christ. The hymn of verses 6 to 11 tells the whole story of the gospel in a few lines: the Son's existence with God, his coming down into human life and death, and his exaltation as Lord. The rest of the chapter shows that story reproduced in ordinary people: Paul poured out like an offering, Timothy caring for others' interests, and Epaphroditus risking his life. Chapter 3 will add Paul's own example of counting his advantages as loss for Christ.
historical:
Philippi was a Roman colony, and its public life honored the emperor. By the time of Paul, emperors were commonly honored with divine titles in the eastern provinces, and after death some were officially declared gods by the Roman Senate. Imperial propaganda celebrated rulers who rose to glory by conquest. Against that background the Christ hymn tells of one who had equality with God and did not use it for his own advantage, who went down to the most shameful death Rome inflicted, and whom God exalted as Lord over all. Readers in a Roman colony could hardly miss the contrast between Caesar and Christ, though the hymn's first purpose is to describe Christ, not to attack Rome.

Epaphroditus (v. 25) was a member of the Philippian church who had brought their gift to Paul and stayed to serve him, and he fell gravely ill. The distance between Philippi and Paul's place of imprisonment, and the several exchanges of news the chapter implies, are part of the debate over where Paul was held. Timothy, who joined Paul shortly before the church was founded (Acts 16:1-3) and was later sent back to Macedonia (Acts 19:22), was well known to the Philippians.
cultural:
Crucifixion was a Roman punishment for slaves, rebels, and the lowest criminals, designed to humiliate as much as to kill. Roman citizens, such as many in Philippi, were normally exempt from it. That is why the hymn's line, “even death on a cross”, is its lowest point: Christ went not only to death but to the death reserved for slaves. The same hymn says he took the form of a servant, the Greek word for slave.

Humility (v. 3) was not generally admired in Greek and Roman culture, where the word usually described the mean-spirited attitude of the lowly; honor and status were pursued openly. Paul makes it a virtue grounded in Christ. The drink offering of verse 17 was a libation of wine poured out alongside a sacrifice, known both in Israel's worship (Numbers 28:7) and in Greek and Roman religion. Paul pictures his possible death as such an offering, poured out on the sacrifice of the Philippians' faith. The complaining and arguing of verse 14 and the crooked and perverse generation of verse 15 echo the language of Israel's grumbling in the wilderness and of Deuteronomy 32:5.
literary: Verses 6 to 11 are written in a poetic, rhythmic style that sets them apart from the surrounding prose, and many scholars think they are an early Christian hymn that Paul quotes, perhaps one the Philippians already knew. Others think Paul composed them himself for this letter. Either way the passage is carefully shaped in two movements. In the first (vv. 6-8) Christ is the subject: he did not grasp, he emptied himself, he humbled himself, going down step by step to death on a cross. In the second (vv. 9-11) God is the subject: he exalted Christ and gave him the name above all names. Verses 10 and 11 echo Isaiah 45:23, where the LORD, the God of Israel, says that to him every knee will bow and every tongue will swear. The chapter around the hymn is built on examples: the appeal (vv. 1-4), the model of Christ (vv. 5-11), the application (vv. 12-18), and two living examples (vv. 19-30).

outline.t: An appeal for unity and humility
Christ emptied himself and humbled himself to death
God exalted him: Jesus Christ is Lord
Work out your salvation; shine as lights

doctrines.note: The hymn confesses that Christ existed in the form of God, possessing equality with God, and truly became human, obedient to death. It is one of the New Testament's clearest witnesses to the church's confession that Jesus Christ is fully God and fully human, one person who came down for our salvation and was raised and exalted.

Verses 10 and 11 apply to Jesus words that Isaiah 45:23 spoke of the LORD alone, yet the confession that Jesus is Lord is to the glory of God the Father. The Son shares the name and honor of the one God while remaining distinct from the Father, a pattern the church later confessed as the Trinity.

Work out your salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you (vv. 12-13). Salvation is not earned, but it is lived out, and the believer's effort is itself the fruit of God's prior work.

Christ was made in human likeness and found in appearance as a man. The Son did not merely seem human; he took on real human life, including obedience and death, which gives human life and humble service a dignity God himself has shared.

words.note: Kenoo, to empty. He emptied himself (v. 7) gives rise to the theological term kenosis. The verb is often used figuratively for making something of no account. The following phrases explain the emptying: taking the form of a servant, being made in human likeness. The church has understood this as the Son humbly taking on human nature and its limits, not ceasing to be God (see the hard question).

Morphe, form. Christ existed in the form of God and took the form of a servant (vv. 6-7). The same word is used in both places, so whatever it means for his being a servant it means for his being God. Most interpreters understand it as a real, outward expression of what someone truly is, not a mere appearance.

Harpagmos, something to be grasped, a rare word found only here in the New Testament. Scholars debate whether it means something not yet possessed and to be seized, or something already possessed and to be held on to or used for one's own advantage. Many now favor the second: Christ had equality with God and did not treat it as something to exploit for himself.

Kurios, Lord. In the Greek Old Testament it regularly stands for the divine name, the LORD. That every tongue will confess that Jesus Christ is Lord (v. 11), in words drawn from Isaiah 45:23, gives Jesus the name and honor that belong to Israel's God alone.

christ: This chapter contains one of the fullest statements of who Christ is and what he has done anywhere in the New Testament. He existed in the form of God and had equality with God before he became human. He emptied himself, not by giving up being God but by taking the form of a servant and being made in human likeness. As a man he humbled himself further, obeying the Father to the point of death on a cross. God therefore exalted him to the highest place and gave him the name above all names, so that every knee in heaven, on earth, and under the earth will bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father. This is the church's confession: the preexistent Son, truly God, became truly human, died, and was raised and exalted. And Paul presents this Christ not only as the object of faith but as the pattern for his people's life together.

hard.q: When Christ “emptied Himself”, did he give up being God?
hard.a:
This is a first-order question, because it concerns who Christ is. The church's historic confession, stated at the Council of Chalcedon in AD 451, is that Christ is one person with two natures, fully divine and fully human, without the divine nature being lost or changed. The text itself supports this reading: Christ existed in the form of God (the verb suggests continuing existence), and the emptying is explained by what he took on, the form of a servant and human likeness, not by anything he gave up. He added humanity rather than subtracting deity. The hymn's ending, where he receives the name and worship due to the LORD, would make little sense if he had ceased to be God.

In the nineteenth century some theologians, particularly in Germany and later in Britain, proposed kenotic theories, holding that the Son laid aside certain divine attributes, such as knowing all things or being present everywhere, in order to live a truly human life. Many orthodox theologians reply that the Son voluntarily limited the use of his divine prerogatives while never ceasing to possess them, which fits the Gospels' picture of a Jesus who grew in wisdom and did not claim to know the day of his return. The question of how the Son's divine and human life relate remains a subject of reflection, but the confession that he is fully God and fully human is the church's settled faith.

questions: Paul asks you to consider others more important than yourself. Where would following Christ's example require you to give up an advantage for someone else's good?
How do verses 12 and 13 help you hold together your own effort and God's work in your life?
Timothy and Epaphroditus are commended for ordinary, costly faithfulness. Who in your life has shown you what the mind of Christ looks like?
